source_text: Ille vero, si quis est cuius causa in congressum descendis scripturarum, ut eum dubitantem confirmes, ad veritatem, an magis ad haereses deverget? Hoc ipso motus, quod te videat nihil promovisse, aequo gradu negandi et defendendi adversa parte, statu certe pari, altercatione incertior discedet, nesciens quam haeresin iudicet. Haec utique et ipsi habent in nos retorquere. Necesse est enim et illos dicere a nobis potius adulteria scripturarum et expositionum mendacia inferri, qui proinde sibi defendant veritatem.
thought_title: The skeptic leaves more uncertain after debate
orientation: Tertullian is addressing a Christian who would debate heretics from Scripture, and now asks what happens to the doubting person for whose sake the debate is entered.
pass_a_gloss: But that man, if there is anyone for whose sake you go down into a contest of the Scriptures, so that you may strengthen him as he doubts, will he incline to the truth, or rather to the heresies? Moved by this very fact, that he sees you have advanced nothing, with the opposing side equal in step of denying and defending, with the standing certainly equal, he will depart more uncertain from the dispute, not knowing which heresy he should judge. These things certainly they also are able to turn back against us. For it is necessary that they also say that by us rather adulterations of the Scriptures and falsehoods of expositions are brought in, who in like manner defend the truth for themselves.

lemmas.gloss: to have advanced, to have made progress
to be brought in, to be introduced

choices.english: you go down into a contest of the Scriptures
choices.why: descendis has the sense of entering a contest or arena; congressum is a meeting or encounter, here adversarial
rejected: you descend to a meeting of the Scriptures
you enter a debate over the Scriptures

choices.english: with the opposing side equal in step of denying and defending
choices.why: aequo gradu is an ablative of manner, 'with equal step'; negandi and defendendi are gerunds showing the two sides' equal ability
rejected: with equal footing in denying and defending
at an equal pace of denial and defense

choices.why: statu is ablative of status, 'standing, position'; pari means equal; certe emphasizes the certainty of the equality
adulteria is plural of adulterium, literally 'adulteries', used metaphorically for corrupting or falsifying texts; the glossary sense of falsehood is captured by the following mendacia
mendacia is the glossary term 'falsehood'; expositionum are interpretations or expositions, matching the earlier context about twisting expositions

pass_b_english: But the person for whose sake you enter a contest over the Scriptures, to steady him when he wavers—will he turn toward the truth, or rather toward heresies? Moved by the very fact that he sees you have made no progress, with the opposing side equal in denying and defending, with the standing certainly equal, the dispute will depart more uncertain, not knowing which heresy to judge. These things, of course, they can also turn back against us. For they too must say that it is rather we who introduce adulterations of the Scriptures and falsehoods of expositions, since they likewise claim the truth for themselves.

problems.quote: he will leave the dispute more uncertain, not knowing which heresy to judge
problems.source_quote: alteratio incertior discedet, nesciens quam haeresin iudicet
problems.why: Latin says the dispute (alteratio) departs more uncertain; English makes the person leave the dispute, changing who acts.
problems.fix: the dispute will depart more uncertain, not knowing which heresy to judge
problems.ruling: Source says altercatio incertior discedet (the dispute departs more uncertain); English makes the person leave, changing the subject and agency.

edits.old: he will leave the dispute more uncertain, not knowing which heresy to judge
edits.new: the dispute will depart more uncertain, not knowing which heresy to judge

fixed: Changed 'he will leave the dispute' to 'the dispute will depart' because the Latin 'alteratio incertior discedet' has the dispute (alteratio) as the subject of discedet, not the person.
